title: Government Budgets and Debt
objective: After this level you can explain deficits, surpluses and national debt.
summary: A deficit is one year's gap between spending and taxes; the national debt is the running total of borrowing plus interest. Economists weigh its risks and uses differently.

cards.headline: In 2015, Britain paid off debts from the 1700s.
cards.body: Some of the old bonds it repaid traced back to the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720 and to borrowing used for the Napoleonic Wars. How does a country end up owing money for nearly three centuries? Start with a single year's budget.

cards.headline: Deficit or surplus
cards.body: Every year, a government compares what it spends with what it collects in taxes. Spend more than it collects, and it runs a budget deficit. Collect more than it spends, and it runs a surplus. If the two match, the budget is balanced. Surpluses don't come around often: the US federal government last ran one in 2001.

cards.headline: The bathtub
cards.body: A deficit is one year's gap; the debt is the running total. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, largely by selling bonds. The national debt is all that borrowing added up, plus the interest owed. Think of a bathtub: the deficit is the tap running this year, the debt is the water level. Borrow $10,000 a year for four years and your yearly deficit is $10,000, but your debt is $40,000.
cards.callout: Deficit: this year's gap. Debt: the total so far.

mascot.line: Deficit and debt get mixed up constantly. The deficit is the tap; the debt is the water level.

cards.headline: How much debt is too much? Economists weigh both sides

items.label: The worry
points: That can leave less for private investment ("crowding out")

items.label: The other view
points: Borrowing can pay for roads, water systems, education and research

options.label: The total a government owes from all past years
A year when a government collects more than it spends
The interest a government pays on its bonds
options.rationale: Interest is part of the debt, not the definition of a deficit.

options.label: A year when a government spends more than it collects in taxes

questions.explanation: A deficit is one year's gap: spending above what taxes bring in.

questions.prompt: A country runs a deficit this year. What happens to its national debt?

options.label: It grows, because the borrowing adds to the total
It shrinks, because the deficit is paid off at year end
options.rationale: A deficit is covered by borrowing, which adds to the debt.

options.label: Nothing: deficits and debt are unrelated
options.rationale: The debt is the running total of past deficits.

options.label: It resets to zero for the new year
options.rationale: The debt carries over; only the deficit is yearly.

questions.explanation: The deficit is the tap, the debt is the water level: a deficit raises the level.

questions.prompt: From Level 51: which big federal spending item gets larger as the national debt grows?

options.label: National defense
options.rationale: Defense is a big item, but it is not a cost of the debt.

options.label: Education
options.rationale: That's mostly state and local spending.

options.label: Social Security
options.rationale: Social Security is funded by payroll taxes, not debt.

questions.explanation: The debt includes interest owed, and interest on past borrowing is one of the biggest federal items.
